content: This updated Cochrane Review, originally published in 2014, focuses on the use of clobazam as monotherapy for individuals with new-onset focal or generalized seizures. The review aims to assess the efficacy, effectiveness, tolerability, and safety of clobazam in this context, while also identifying gaps in the current evidence base. To conduct this review, a comprehensive search of multiple databases was performed on March 19, 2018. These databases included the Cochrane Register of Studies (CRS Web), MEDLINE, BIOSIS Previews, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP). No restrictions were placed on language. The inclusion criteria required randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials comparing clobazam monotherapy to either placebo or other anti-seizure medications in individuals with two or more unprovoked seizures or a single acute symptomatic seizure requiring short-term continuous anti-seizure treatment. The primary outcome measure was the time participants remained on their allocated treatment (retention time), which reflects both efficacy and tolerability. Secondary outcomes included measures of shortand long-term effectiveness, tolerability, quality of life, and tolerance. Data extraction was performed independently by two authors. The review identified three trials that met the inclusion criteria, involving a total of 206 participants. However, none of these studies reported the preselected primary outcome measure, and a meta-analysis could not be conducted. The quality of evidence was downgraded for some results due to concerns about allocation concealment and a high risk of performance and detection bias in two of the studies, as assessed using the GRADE approach. Regarding retention at 12 months, there was no statistically significant difference between clobazam and carbamazepine (risk ratio [RR] 0.83, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.61 to 1.12; low-quality evidence). However, low-quality evidence suggested that clobazam may have better retention compared to phenytoin (RR 1.43, 95% CI 1.08 to 1.90). It was unclear whether participants receiving clobazam were less likely to discontinue treatment due to adverse effects compared to those receiving phenytoin (RR 0.10, 95% CI 0.01 to 1.65; low-quality evidence). The authors concluded that there is no clear advantage of clobazam over carbamazepine for retention at 12 months in drug-naive children. A slight advantage of clobazam over phenytoin for retention at six months was observed in adolescents and adults with neurocysticercosis, but this finding was based on a single clinical trial. Overall, the available evidence is insufficient to guide clinical practice regarding the use of clobazam as monotherapy for new-onset focal or generalized seizures.
